synopsis: The programme is a first-time capability build under high technical uncertainty: sensor types, machine types, software maturity and existing recordings were unavailable, supplier cooperation remains unknown, and an unconfirmed sensor choice is identified as the largest schedule risk [f9401, f8, f10801, f1618]. Its main technical risk is the absence of a published quantitative off-road comparison between simulation-tuned braking thresholds and field results; statistical methods cannot compensate for omitted hazards, incorrect exposure models or an unvalidated simulator [f155, f5952, f650, f994]. The recommended approach combines evidence-based stage gates with assumption-based and discovery-driven planning, tracking vulnerable assumptions, failure signposts and hedges while keeping verified facts, expert judgment and management assumptions separate [f203, f9591, f9558, f12277]. This recommendation is not proof of effectiveness: evidence for risk-management outcomes is thin, a 2010 meta-analysis found positive impacts in only two of 29 publications, and rigorous comparative evidence for assumption-based planning was not found [f9440, f9441, f9562]. Supplier-data availability and legal usability, evolving interfaces, facility access and standards changes require explicit treatment; planning should not depend on an off-road scenario standard arriving before mid-2027, and outsourcing needs editable models and validation assets to avoid long-term dependency [f11024, f8619, f1167, f11222, f7205, f8799]. Important unresolved questions include the causes of prior three-to-four-year development timelines, market-dependent EU applicability, security and privacy obligations, and cloud/export/data-residency terms; these gaps should prompt manufacturer questions, supplier requests or early experiments rather than invented estimates [f11185, f10854, f10701, f10823, f16068, f263, f6631].
